title: Implementation, Ad-hoc & Constructive
relevance: High — tests raw coding fluency, edge-case handling, and translating logic into bug-free code—the most common reason candidates fail OAs.
company_notes: Amazon/Microsoft grid-traversal OAs: simulate robots and obstacles in 2D without BFS/DFS. Citadel/Optiver/HRT game simulations: predict the winner after N turns, often an O(1) parity or ad-hoc math disguise. Google/Meta array/string transformations: apply replacement rules until stable—find the invariant or shrink-to-pattern. Data-engineering/pipeline OAs: parse logs and compute active-session streaks—pure implementation and edge cases.

phases.goal: Establish that the problem is simulation, ad-hoc math, or constructive—not advanced DS or a textbook algorithm.

must_hit.point: These problems need simulating a process, finding a mathematical shortcut (ad-hoc), or building a valid configuration from scratch (constructive)—not advanced data structures or textbook algorithms.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names simulation, ad-hoc shortcut, or constructive build as the family and rejects jumping to heavy DS/algos.

must_hit.point: Recognition cues: constraints small enough for direct simulation, or the ask is “any valid answer” with room for a surprisingly simple greedy construction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Points at small constraints for simulate-directly, or “any valid” wording that invites a simple greedy builder.

must_hit.point: OA disguises include grid robot/obstacle movement without BFS/DFS, game winner-after-N-turns prompts, replacement rules until a string stops changing, and log streak/session counting.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps the prompt to grid sim, game-after-N-turns, invariant/shrink string transforms, or streak parsing.

probes: What in the statement says this is simulation, ad-hoc math, or constructive rather than a standard DS/algorithm template?
Would you treat this as “simulate everything” or as “any valid construction,” and why?

hints.1: Ask whether you need a fancy structure or just to run the process / emit one valid object.
hints.2: Look for small constraints (direct simulation) or “any valid answer” (simple greedy construction).
hints.3: Classify as simulate / O(1) math shortcut / construct-any; OA cousins are grid move sims, N-turn games, replacement-until-stable strings, and streak parsing.

phases.goal: Choose simulate vs ad-hoc formula vs construct-any, and name the invariant or base-case reduction before coding.

must_hit.point: Prefer an O(1) math formula or division/modulo logic that dictates the exact state at step N over blind O(N) simulation when the pattern allows it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says to hunt an O(1)/modulo closed form (e.g. grid pattern or k-th not-divisible jump) instead of looping every step.

must_hit.point: For “does there exist” or “construct any,” reduce to the most extreme or simplest valid base case (e.g. sorting, placing all 1s together).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names reducing to a simplest skeleton like sorted order or all-1s-together before inventing a bespoke search.

must_hit.point: Hunt invariants that never change under the operations—e.g. sum modulo K or parity of inversions—especially on string/array transforms and games.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sum modulo K, parity, or another unchanged quantity before proposing per-step simulation.

must_hit.point: Constructive stretch patterns include reducing a general case (k>3) to a solved base case (k=3), and reverse-thinking such as blocking bad cells instead of helping the good path.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites k>3→k=3 reduction or block-the-bad-guys framing when the problem is constructive.

probes: Before coding, is the win condition a simulation, an O(1) formula, or any valid construction?
What invariant or simplest valid base case would you reduce to?

hints.1: Don’t start looping every step until you’ve asked for a closed form or a construct-any skeleton.
hints.2: Either derive O(1)/modulo state at step N, or reduce existence/construction to a simplest base (sort / all 1s together).
hints.3: Name an invariant (sum modulo K, parity) and, if stretch, k>3→k=3 or block-bad-guys reverse thinking.

phases.goal: Show concrete coding moves for grids, strings/digits, in-place markers, and common constructive builders.

must_hit.point: 2D grids need boundary checks and 4-way/8-way directional arrays; spiral/diagonal walks must track cycle bounds carefully.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions bounds checks, directional deltas, and careful spiral/diagonal loop limits.

must_hit.point: Treat strings and numbers as digit arrays with explicit leading-zero and parity handling (e.g. digit inversion that must not create a leading zero).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Talks digit-array edits and calls out leading zeros / parity as first-class edge cases.

must_hit.point: In-place matrix work can use the first row/column as state markers to achieve O(1) space modification (Set Matrix Zeroes pattern).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes marking on the first row/column instead of extra O(rows+cols) arrays.

must_hit.point: Core builders include streak/sliding-window counts, bracket balance tracking, frequency-counting for symmetric/palindrome construction, and bottleneck gaps such as max distance between 'R's.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names streak counting, balance for brackets, frequency→symmetric string, or max 'R' gap as the coded idea.

probes: How would you implement an in-place matrix zeroing without an extra marker array?
What edge cases do you check when mutating digits of a number as a string?

hints.1: Start from grid deltas or digit-array edits—whichever the prompt looks like.
hints.2: Grids: boundaries + 4-way/8-way; matrices: first row/column markers for O(1) space; strings: leading zeros.
hints.3: Also mention spiral cycle bounds, bracket balance, frequency→palindrome layout, or max distance between 'R's.

phases.goal: State when simulation is acceptable versus when an O(1) formula or O(1)-space in-place pass is required.

must_hit.point: When an O(1) formula or division/modulo logic gives the state at step N, O(N) simulation is the wrong complexity choice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts closed-form/modulo O(1) answers with looping N steps unnecessarily.

must_hit.point: Space-optimized matrix problems may require O(1) space in-place modification rather than auxiliary row/column arrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says O(1) extra space via first-row/column markers for zeroing or similar.

must_hit.point: Game-style OA prompts that ask for the winner after N turns often collapse to an O(1) parity check or ad-hoc math trick rather than simulating all turns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Refuses full N-turn simulation and proposes parity/ad-hoc O(1) reasoning.

probes: When is simulating all N steps acceptable, and when should you switch to an O(1) formula?
What space bound are you aiming for on in-place matrix modification?

hints.1: Ask whether the answer depends on every intermediate state or only on a closed form.
hints.2: Prefer O(1) math/parity when the pattern or game rules allow; reserve simulation for small-constraint process walks.
hints.3: Cite O(1) jump/formula vs O(N) loop, O(1) space via first row/column markers, and N-turn games that hide parity.

phases.goal: Surface the edge-case and wrong-framing mistakes that fail OAs on this topic.

must_hit.point: Off-by-one and loop-bound errors dominate spiral/diagonal matrix traversal and similar cycle-bound walks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out spiral/diagonal off-by-one and shrinking bounds as the main failure mode.

must_hit.point: Digit/string mutations often break on leading zeros and parity edge cases if those checks are skipped.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly tests or mentions leading-zero and parity traps on digit flips.

must_hit.point: Missing 2D boundary checks (or wrong 4-way/8-way deltas) corrupts grid simulations even when the high-level idea is right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions out-of-bounds indices or incorrect neighbor directions as a concrete bug class.

must_hit.point: On constructive/BFS maze variants, helping only the good path can be the wrong frame—blocking the bad guys first is the intended reverse-thinking.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States block-bad-cells / reverse approach instead of only clearing a path for the hero.

probes: Where do candidates usually go off-by-one on spiral or layered matrix walks?
What happens if you invert digits without considering a leading zero?

hints.1: Think bounds and first/last cells before the happy-path loop.
hints.2: Spiral cycle bounds, grid boundaries/deltas, and leading zeros are the usual OA killers.
hints.3: Also: don’t O(N)-simulate an O(1) pattern; on maze constructives, block bad guys rather than only helping good guys.

tradeoffs.topic: O(N) simulation vs O(1) ad-hoc math
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If division/modulo or a closed formula gives the exact state at step N (Number Spiral, K-th Not Divisible, Coin Piles, many N-turn games), prefer O(1); simulate only when constraints make direct process walking the intended path.

tradeoffs.topic: Pure 2D implementation vs reaching for BFS/DFS
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Grid-traversal OAs that only move robots among obstacles often test boundary-safe 2D implementation with directional arrays—not graph search. Use BFS/DFS only when reachability/search is actually required.

tradeoffs.topic: Construct any simple skeleton vs searching for a special solution
tradeoffs.strong_answer: When the problem asks for any valid answer and constraints are loose (e.g. forcing periodicity), emit the simplest greedy construction or extreme base case rather than searching for a unique or optimal-looking object.

tradeoffs.topic: Solve the general constructive case vs reduce to a known base
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Patterns like k-LCM hard reduce k>3 to the already-solved k=3 case; prefer that reduction over inventing a full general builder from scratch.

tradeoffs.topic: Help the good path vs block the bad guys
tradeoffs.strong_answer: On Solve The Maze–style constructives, reverse-thinking—block bad cells so evil cannot reach the goal—beats only trying to clear a path for the good side.

gotchas.trap: Tracing spirals or diagonals with wrong cycle bounds.
gotchas.correction: Track shrinking layer bounds carefully; off-by-one on loop limits is the classic spiral-matrix OA failure.

gotchas.trap: Mutating digits without guarding leading zeros.
gotchas.correction: Treat the number as a digit array and refuse transforms that introduce a leading zero; parity/edge cases belong in the same checklist.

gotchas.trap: Simulating all N steps when an O(1) formula exists.
gotchas.correction: Use division/modulo or parity that dictates the state at step N (grid formulas, k-th not-divisible jumps, many game winner prompts).

gotchas.trap: Grid simulation without boundary checks or correct 4-way/8-way deltas.
gotchas.correction: Validate every neighbor index and keep directional arrays consistent before applying moves.

gotchas.trap: Applying string replacement rules step-by-step without an invariant.
gotchas.correction: Find what never changes (e.g. sum modulo K, parity) or recognize the string shrinks to a known pattern instead of brute-forcing every replacement.

gotchas.trap: Allocating extra row/column marker arrays when O(1) space is required.
gotchas.correction: Use the first row/column as state markers for in-place matrix zeroing and similar modifications.

gotchas.trap: Framing a maze constructive as only helping the good cells.
gotchas.correction: Block the bad guys (reverse-thinking) so adversarial reachability fails, rather than only paving the hero’s path.
